name: Great Moravia
info: The first major West Slavic state, centred on the Morava River, where Cyril and Methodius created the Glagolitic alphabet and the Slavonic liturgy before the Hungarians overran it.

facts.capital: Not identified: the sources' Veligrad is unlocated, and Mikulčice is the most widely accepted candidate; Nitra was the centre of the eastern part
facts.founder: Mojmír I, the first known ruler of the united Moravia (r. 820s/830s–846)
facts.predecessor: The Slavic tribes north of the Danube under Avar influence (Samo's tribal union 631–658, the Avar Khaganate 567–822) and the Principality of Nitra under Pribina
facts.successor: The Principality of Hungary (the Hungarians, 902–907), later the Kingdom of Hungary and the Kingdom of Bohemia

t: Rastislav asked Constantinople for teachers in 863 to free his church from Frankish priests; the mission of Cyril and Methodius gave the Slavs their first alphabet and liturgy.
Moravia reached its greatest extent under Svatopluk I (870–894), when Bohemia, Pannonia and Lesser Poland at least formally accepted his suzerainty.
Pope John VIII's bull Industriae tuae of 880 recognised Old Church Slavonic as the fourth liturgical language, beside Latin, Greek and Hebrew.
dyk: Great Moravia's capital has never been found: the sources name a Veligrad, and Mikulčice, with its palace and twelve churches on an island in the Morava, is the most widely accepted candidate.
ev: Mojmír I, duke of the Moravians, expels Pribina from Nitra across the Danube; the union of Nitra with Moravia makes Great Moravia.
Louis the German campaigns against the Moravians and installs Mojmír's nephew Rastislav as duke.
At Rastislav's request Emperor Michael III sends Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius, who bring the Glagolitic alphabet and the Slavonic liturgy.
The Moravians rise against the Frankish governors William and Engelschalk; Svatopluk returns, leads the revolt and drives the Franks out.
Pope John VIII's bull Industriae tuae takes Svatopluk under papal protection, confirms Methodius as archbishop and recognises Old Church Slavonic in the liturgy.
Methodius dies on 6 April; Bishop Wiching of Nitra has the Slavonic rite restricted and, in 886, Methodius's disciples expelled.
Svatopluk I dies in the summer; under his son Mojmír II the subjugated tribes begin to break away.
No Moravian force fights at Brezalauspurc, where the Hungarians rout the Bavarians; the Moravian state has ceased to exist between 902 and 907.

sections.foundation:
Great Moravia was the first major state that was predominantly West Slavic, centred on the Morava River, which gave it its name, in today's eastern Czech Republic and western Slovakia. The local Slavs, long tributary to the Avars, built their first fortified settlements in the late seventh century. Charlemagne's campaigns in the 790s broke the Avar Khaganate, and Frankish swords and Carolingian art spread north of the Middle Danube. Fortresses at Bratislava, Rajhrad and Staré Město around 800 mark local centres of power.

The Royal Frankish Annals record “leaders of the Slavs who live along the Danube” at Louis the Pious's court in 811 and embassies of Moravians at Frankfurt in 822, the earliest certain reference to them. The first named ruler is Mojmír I, “duke of the Moravians”, who according to the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum expelled Pribina across the Danube; Pribina fled to Ratpot, who administered the March of Pannonia from around 833. Whether Pribina was an independent prince of Nitra or Mojmír's lieutenant is disputed, but many historians hold that Great Moravia emerged through the enforced union of Nitra with Moravia in the early 830s. A thirteenth-century source says Bishop Reginhar of Passau baptised “all of the Moravians” in 831. In 846 Louis the German marched against Moravians “planning to defect” and installed Mojmír's nephew Rastislav as duke.
sections.socioeconomy:
The nuclei of settlement were large fortified strongholds on hills, marshes and river islands, with ramparts of drystone facing and earth-filled timber frames, the elite in the central enclosure and crafts in the outer ones. Three agglomerations, Mikulčice-Valy, Staré Město–Uherské Hradiště and Nitra, formed huge fortified pre-urban centres; Mikulčice's acropolis on an island in the Morava enclosed six hectares with a palace and twelve churches, and Nitra had some twenty craftsmen's villages. Around the forts lay villages growing wheat, barley and millet and farming cattle, pigs, sheep and horses no larger than Przewalski horses.

Two trade routes, the Danube and the ancient Amber Road, crossed the region. Iron metallurgy and smithing were the chief industries. Moravia had no silver, gold, copper or lead mines, so jewellery and weapons were made from metal won as loot, gift or trade; no local coinage is known, and axe-shaped ingots may have served as a premonetary currency. Silk, brocade and glass vessels were imported, and the Moravians paid chiefly in slaves taken as prisoners of war: Archbishop Thietmar of Salzburg accused them of “bringing noble men and honest women into slavery” in Pannonia, and the Raffelstetten Customs Regulations record slaves sent west from Moravia. Most people were freemen paying an annual tax; slavery and feudal dependency are also recorded.
sections.military:
The core of the army was the družina, a princely retinue of professional warriors, some as his permanent guard and the rest garrisoned in forts; Ruttkay estimates it at 3,000–5,000 men. Its permanent part was cavalry, heavy horsemen modelled on the Frankish forerunners of knights with equipment only the richest could afford. In large mobilisations the retinues of local magnates and the pohotovosť of free commoners joined, perhaps 20,000–30,000 men in all, fighting mainly in defence under the prince or a voivode. The foot soldier's weapon was the bradatica axe; double-edged swords spread, and Avar sabres and reflex bows are absent.

Fortifications were the backbone of defence. Louis the German invaded in 855 and withdrew before “strong fortifications”; in 864 he besieged Rastislav in Dowina and could not take it; in 869 Charles burnt the walled places of the region but failed before Rastislav's “huge fortification, quite unlike any built in olden times”. In 871 the Moravians rose against the Frankish governors William and Engelschalk, elected Slavomír duke and, under the returning Svatopluk, drove the Franks out; in 872 Svatopluk's army defeated imperial troops and forced their withdrawal. He invaded Pannonia during the Wilhelminer War of 882–884 with “troops from all the Slav lands”, seized a pagan prince on the Vistula, and in 892 withstood King Arnulf's invasion although Magyar horsemen rode with the Franks.
sections.governance:
Moravia was ruled by the House of Mojmír, a “wider kinship” rather than a line of fathers and sons: Svatopluk I was the only ruler succeeded by his son, Rastislav owed his throne to Louis the German, and Slavomír, an ordained priest, was elected duke when the Franks held Svatopluk in 871. Rulers were styled dux, occasionally rex or malik, and Pope Stephen V addressed Svatopluk as “King of the Slavs” in 885. Whether the realm was organised by kinship or by counties under zhupans is debated. The realm had two centres, and Nitra was held as an appanage by the heir, Svatopluk under his uncle Rastislav. A council of “leading men”, optimates, sat with the monarch.

Religion was bound up with sovereignty. Frankish priests served East Francia's interests, so in 861 Rastislav asked Pope Nicholas I for missionaries who knew Slavic and, receiving no answer, turned to Emperor Michael III, who sent Constantine and Methodius in 863. In 880 John VIII's bull Industriae tuae placed Svatopluk under papal protection and confirmed Methodius over all clergy, yet at Svatopluk's request named his opponent Wiching bishop of Nitra. Methodius also gave Moravia its only surviving laws, the Nomocanon, a translation of Byzantine canon law, and the Court Law for the People. After his death in 885 Wiching persuaded the pope to restrict the Slavonic rite and Svatopluk to expel his disciples in 886.
sections.impact:
Great Moravia's lasting mark was made in letters. Constantine, later Saint Cyril, devised the Glagolitic alphabet, the first dedicated to a Slavic language, and with Methodius translated the Gospel and then, in Methodius's words, “all the Scriptures in full, save Maccabees” into Old Church Slavonic, which became the fourth liturgical language of Christendom. Though the Slavic liturgy lasted only about 22 years in Moravia, the disciples expelled in 886 carried it to Bulgaria, Croatia and Bohemia; at the Preslav Literary School Bulgarian disciples such as Naum and Clement of Ohrid created the Cyrillic alphabet, which became the script of the Bulgarian Empire and Kievan Rus', and Old Church Slavonic remains the liturgical language of several Orthodox churches.

Moravia's churches, more than 25 identified in the core lands, ranged from three-nave basilicas at Mikulčice and Bratislava to rotundas; its granulated earrings and gilded buttons formed a recognisable jewellery style. Politically it was the first West Slavic state and reached early feudalism, the social basis of the later medieval kingdoms of the region. In the nineteenth century Great Moravia became a theme of Czech and Slovak romantic nationalism, in the twentieth it served a Czechoslovak identity, and it is named in the preamble of Slovakia's constitution; the double cross thought to have come with Cyril and Methodius is in Slovakia's arms.
sections.decline:
Svatopluk died in the summer of 894, and his son Mojmír II inherited a realm that soon came apart, as the tribes forced under Moravian rule shook it off. The Bohemian dukes accepted King Arnulf's suzerainty in June 895 and Mojmír's attempts to win them back failed. War with his younger brother Svatopluk II gave Arnulf a pretext to send troops in 898 and 899; Bavarian forces rescued the “boy” Svatopluk from the dungeon where his brother held him and, by Bartl's account, destroyed the fortress of Nitra.

The Hungarians, beaten on the Pontic steppes around 895 by Bulgars and Pechenegs, were moving into the Carpathian Basin. Around 900 Moravians and Bavarians accused each other of swearing alliances with them “by the means of a dog and a wolf”, and a large Hungarian army “attacked and invaded” Moravia in 900. Mojmír II made peace with Louis the Child in 901. The end cannot be dated: Róna-Tas puts the Hungarian occupation in 902, Spinei in 903 or 904, Spiesz the state's extinction in 907; the Raffelstetten Customs Regulations of 903–906 still speak of “the markets of the Moravians”, and no Moravian force fought at Brezalauspurc in 907, where the Hungarians routed the Bavarians. Its lands passed to Hungary and Bohemia, the Slavic population stayed in the Carpathian valleys, Moravia is still mentioned in 924/925 and 942, and only the chapel at Kopčany still stands from its time.

summary: Great Moravia, the first major West Slavic state, grew under Mojmír I, Rastislav and Svatopluk I along the Morava River from the 830s, received the mission of Cyril and Methodius in 863 and with it the Glagolitic alphabet and the Slavonic liturgy, reached its widest extent around 890, and fell to internal strife and the Hungarians between 902 and 907.
references: A. P. Vlasto, The Entry of the Slavs into Christendom: An Introduction to the Medieval History of the Slavs (Cambridge University Press, 1970)
Florin Curta, Southeastern Europe in the Middle Ages, 500–1250 (Cambridge University Press, 2006)

pointDescs.833: Mojmír I expels Pribina from Nitra across the Danube; Pribina flees to Ratpot, who administers the March of Pannonia from around 833. The union of Nitra with Moravia makes Great Moravia.
pointDescs.846: Around 15 August Louis the German campaigns against the Moravians, “who were planning to defect”, and installs Mojmír's nephew Rastislav as duke.
pointDescs.855: Louis the German invades after Rastislav backs the rebel Radbod; the Moravians, “defended by strong fortifications”, hold out, and a peace in 859 is a stalemate that shows the realm's growing strength.
pointDescs.864: Louis the German besieges Rastislav in Dowina and cannot take it, but Rastislav accepts his suzerainty while continuing to support the king's opponents.
pointDescs.869: Frankish armies under Charles and Carloman burn the walled places of Moravia and lay waste Svatopluk's lands, but fail before Rastislav's main fortress and withdraw.
pointDescs.871: After Svatopluk helps the Franks seize Rastislav in 870 and is himself arrested, the Moravians rise against the governors William and Engelschalk; Svatopluk returns, leads them and drives the Franks out.
pointDescs.874: After defeating imperial troops in 872, Svatopluk makes peace at Forchheim, promising fidelity and a yearly tribute to Louis the German; Methodius returns and is given all the churches and clergy of Moravia.
pointDescs.880: Pope John VIII's bull Industriae tuae calls Svatopluk “the only son” of the Holy See, confirms Methodius over all clergy and recognises Old Church Slavonic as a liturgical language; Wiching becomes bishop of Nitra.
pointDescs.884: Svatopluk invades Pannonia during the Wilhelminer War and meets Emperor Charles the Fat at Tulln, swearing fidelity as his vassal; Pope Stephen V will address him as King of the Slavs in 885.
pointDescs.890: King Arnulf gives Svatopluk command of the Bohemians; Silesia and Lusatia are probably annexed in the early 890s. Moravia is at its greatest extent, and Arnulf's invasion of 892 fails.
pointDescs.894: Svatopluk I dies in the summer; his son Mojmír II succeeds, but the tribes subjugated by force begin to throw off Moravian supremacy.
pointDescs.895: The Bohemian dukes accept King Arnulf's suzerainty in June; Mojmír II cannot restore his rule over them in the next two years.
pointDescs.899: In the war between Mojmír II and his brother Svatopluk II, Bavarian troops free the “boy” Svatopluk from his dungeon and, by Bartl's account, destroy the fortress of Nitra.
pointDescs.901: After a large Hungarian army attacks Moravia in 900, Mojmír II makes peace with Louis the Child; Moravians and Bavarians accuse each other of pagan oaths with the Hungarians.
pointDescs.907: The Hungarians rout a large Bavarian force at Brezalauspurc without any Moravian army in the field; the Moravian state has ceased to exist at some point between 902 and 907.

notes: The register's start 833 is read as the union of Nitra with Moravia: the article dates it only to 'the early 830s', with Ratpot administering Pannonia 'from around 833'; the event is written 'c. 833'.
The capital is unknown; the facts box says so rather than naming Mikulčice as fact.

The article's bibliography sections are empty in the saved text, so references is []; it names scholars (Havlík, Třeštík, Vlasto, Kirschbaum, Macháček, Štefan, Bowlus, Barford, Curta) without titles. The external links list Záborský's Dejiny Veľkej Moravy a počiatky Uhorska (Matica slovenská, 1929).

The location of the state is disputed (southern theories of Boba, Bowlus, Eggers); the profile follows the traditional view the article says most historians hold, and the note on the debate is left out of the sections for space.
The end year 907 is the latest of the article's three dates (902, 903/904, 907); the last point and event say the state ended between 902 and 907.
